entry: Establishment where people engage in sexual activity with sex workers, typically for payment. Prostitution and brothels are illegal in many countries, though known illegal brothels may be tolerated, and they often operate as massage parlors, saunas or spas. In a few countries they are legal and regulated. Parties to a 1949 United Nations convention, ratified by 82 states by December 2013, agreed to ban brothels and procuring. The [[Netherlands]] and Germany have liberal [[Prostitution|prostitution]] laws; [[Amsterdam]] is known for its [[Red-light district|red-light district]], and the largest brothel in Europe is the Pascha in [[Cologne]].

Man or boy who shares one or more parents with another person; a male [[Sibling|sibling]]. The female counterpart is a [[Sister]]. The term, which derives from Proto-Indo-European through [[Latin]] *frater*, is sometimes used endearingly for non-relatives. A full brother is a first-degree relative. Some studies suggest that girls with an older brother reach menarche about a year later. In *Nicomachean Ethics*, written in 350 BCE, [[Aristotle]] held that the older brother should shape the younger's ethics through good action, because habits formed early become entrenched. Full brothers share both parents, while half-brothers share one.

German academics, [[Linguistics|linguists]] and folklorists, brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm. Their first collection of folk tales, *Children's and Household Tales* (*Kinder- und Hausmärchen*), was published in 1812; it grew from 86 stories to more than 200 across later editions. Their tales popularized [[Cinderella]], [[Hansel and Gretel]] and [[Rumpelstiltskin]]. They also studied Germanic and Scandinavian legends and medieval texts, and began the historical German dictionary *Deutsches Wörterbuch* in 1838; it was left unfinished at their deaths. Their methods for documenting [[Oral tradition|oral traditions]] set lasting standards for folklore studies. [[Romanticism]] had revived interest in folk stories, which the brothers regarded as a pure form of national literature.

Private [[Ivy League]] research university in [[Providence, Rhode Island]]. Founded in 1764 as the College in the English Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, it is the seventh-oldest higher education institution in the United States and one of nine colonial colleges chartered before the [[American Revolution]]. It has the oldest applied mathematics program in the country and the oldest engineering program in the Ivy League. Its Open Curriculum, adopted in 1969, abolished mandatory general education requirements. As of October 2025, 12 [[Nobel Prize]] laureates had been affiliated with Brown as alumni, faculty or researchers.

Large group of multicellular [[Algae|algae]] comprising the class Phaeophyceae. Between 1,500 and 2,000 species are known. Brown algae are the major seaweeds of temperate and polar regions, and many grow in colder waters of the [[Northern Hemisphere]]. Most live in marine environments, where giant [[Kelp|kelp]] (*Macrocystis pyrifera*) is the largest of all algae and forms underwater forests. Floating mats of *Sargassum* form habitats in the [[Sargasso Sea]]. Brown algae belong to the [[Stramenopile|Stramenopiles]], not closely related to [[Red algae|red algae]] or [[Green algae|green algae]]. Most contain the pigment fucoxanthin, which gives them their color. Unlike other stramenopiles, they develop multicellular forms with differentiated tissues, and they contribute to [[Carbon|carbon]] fixation.

Large [[Bear|bear]] species, *Ursus arctos*, native to [[Eurasia]] and [[North America]]. Rivaled in size on land only by its closest relative, the [[Polar bear]], it is sexually dimorphic, with adult males larger and more compactly built than females. Its fur ranges from cream to reddish to dark brown. Contrary to popular belief, about 90% of its diet is plant matter, though it hunts animals from insects and rodents to [[Moose]]. In coastal Alaska it feeds largely on spawning [[Salmon]]. Solitary for most of the year, it has an average lifespan of 25 years in the wild. It is listed as least concern by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, with an estimated population of 110,000 in 2017, but the Himalayan brown bear is critically endangered.

Substellar object of 13 to 80 times the mass of [[Jupiter]], heavier than the largest [[Gas giant|gas giants]] but lighter than the least massive main-sequence [[Star|stars]]. Too small to sustain hydrogen fusion, it briefly fuses [[Deuterium|deuterium]], and the most massive brown dwarfs, above 65 Jupiter masses, can fuse [[Lithium|lithium]]. As they cool over time, they pass through the spectral types M, L, T and Y, and they emit most of their light in the [[Infrared|infrared]]. Jill Tarter proposed the name in 1975, using brown for a color between red and black. The nearest known brown dwarfs form the Luhman 16 system, about 6.5 [[Light-year|light-years]] from the [[Sun]].

[[Color]], a darker, typically desaturated shade of [[Orange (colour)|orange]]. In the RGB model used for screens, brown is made from red light at medium to low intensity, green at a lower intensity and little blue. In CMYK printing, it is usually made from yellow ink with smaller amounts of [[Magenta]] and black. Minerals, soil and wood are often brown, and many animals have brown pelts, scales or feathers for [[Camouflage|camouflage]]. Brown has been used in art since prehistoric times; paintings made with umber, a clay pigment of iron oxide and manganese oxide, date to 40,000 BC. [[Leonardo da Vinci]], [[Raphael]] and other Renaissance artists used it. The first recorded use of brown as a color name in English was in 1000.

Widespread, common species of [[Rat|rat]], also called the common rat, sewer rat or Norway rat. One of the largest muroids, it is brown or gray, up to 28 cm long, and weighs 140 to 500 g. It is thought to have originated in northern China and has spread to all continents except [[Antarctica]]. It is the dominant rat in [[Europe]] and much of [[North America]], and it lives wherever humans live, particularly in cities. Omnivorous and fast-breeding, it can carry several human diseases. Selective breeding produced the fancy rat and the laboratory rat, a [[Model organism|model organism]] in biological research. Despite its name, it did not originate in Norway.

Recluse spider with [[Venom|necrotic venom]], native to the central United States. Usually 6 to 20 mm long, it is light to medium brown with a dark, violin-shaped marking on its cephalothorax, earning it the names fiddleback spider and violin spider. Its native range runs from southeastern [[Nebraska]] and southern [[Iowa]] south to [[Texas]] and east to [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]. Bites sometimes require medical attention; it and the black widow are the two spiders in North America with dangerous venom. Many reports from outside its range are misidentifications: of 581 spiders submitted from California as brown recluses, only one was a brown recluse.

Random motion of particles suspended in a [[Liquid|liquid]] or [[Gas|gas]]. It is named after Scottish botanist Robert Brown, who described it in 1827 while observing pollen in water under a microscope. [[Albert Einstein]] explained it in 1905 as the result of collisions with individual water molecules, and Jean Perrin verified it experimentally in 1908. The explanation provided convincing evidence that [[Atom|atoms]] and [[Molecule|molecules]] exist. Its traditional mathematical formulation is the Wiener process, a [[Stochastic process|stochastic process]].

City in [[Texas]], United States, and county seat of Cameron County (pop., 2020: 186,738). Located on the Gulf Coast beside Matamoros, Mexico, it was founded in 1848 by Charles Stillman and named for Fort Brown, itself named for Major Jacob Brown, who died during the war. The city was the site of the siege of Fort Texas in the [[Mexican–American War|Mexican–American War]] and of several [[American Civil War|Civil War]] engagements. Its deep-water port handles international trade, and its population is predominantly Hispanic, at 93.9%, the fourth-highest proportion of any U.S. city outside Puerto Rico.

Hong Kong and American [[Martial arts|martial artist]], actor and filmmaker. Born in [[San Francisco]] and raised in Hong Kong, he began as a child actor. He taught martial arts in [[Seattle]] and [[Oakland, California|Oakland]] before moving to Los Angeles, where his students included [[Chuck Norris]] and [[Sharon Tate]]. He founded Jeet Kune Do, a philosophy drawn from unarmed fighting and self-defense and from [[Zen]], Buddhist and Taoist thought. His films *The Big Boss* (1971), *Fist of Fury* (1972) and *Enter the Dragon* (1973) helped popularize Hong Kong action cinema. Regarded as the first global Chinese film star, he died at 32 of brain edema, a cause still disputed. [[Time (magazine)|Time magazine]] named him one of the 100 most important people of the 20th century.

American singer-songwriter and musician, nicknamed the Boss. Springsteen has released 21 studio albums, most featuring the E Street Band, his backing band since 1972. *Born to Run* (1975) brought him worldwide popularity, and *Born in the U.S.A.* (1984) is his most successful album. *The Rising* (2002) was dedicated to the victims of the [[September 11 attacks]]. He has sold more than 140 million records and won 20 [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]]. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1999, and in 2010 [[Rolling Stone]] ranked him 23rd among the greatest artists of all time.

Retired American actor known for action films. He gained fame in the comedy-drama series *Moonlighting* (1985–1989) and became an action hero as John McClane in the *Die Hard* franchise (1988–2013). His other films include *Pulp Fiction* (1994), *Armageddon* (1998) and *The Sixth Sense* (1999). He received a Golden Globe Award, two Primetime Emmy Awards and a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2006. He retired in 2022 because of [[Aphasia|aphasia]], and was diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia in 2023.

City, capital of West Flanders province, Belgium (pop., 2025: 119,765). Its medieval historic center has been a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] since 2000. Bruges is sometimes called the [[Venice]] of the North, along with [[Amsterdam]] and [[Saint Petersburg]]. Once one of the world's chief commercial cities, it declined from the 15th century as the Zwin estuary silted up and choked its port access. It draws over 8 million visitors a year and is the seat of the College of Europe.

Type of hematoma in which capillaries damaged by trauma leak blood into the surrounding tissue. Also called a contusion, a bruise usually results from [[Blunt trauma|blunt trauma]]. The blood stays visible near the skin's surface until tissues absorb it or the [[Immune system|immune system]] clears it. Color ranges from red, blue or almost black depending on severity, and older bruises turn yellow, green or brown. If trauma breaks the skin, the injury is bleeding rather than a bruise. Petechiae, under 3 mm, and purpura, 3 to 10 mm, look similar. Ecchymoses, over 1 cm across, are often treated as a synonym for a larger bruise.

Country in Southeast Asia, on the northern coast of [[Borneo]] (pop., 2025: 466,330). It is the only sovereign state entirely on Borneo and the least populous country in Asia. It is an absolute monarchy ruled by Sultan [[Hassanal Bolkiah]] since 1967, and its legal system combines English common law with Islamic jurisprudence, including [[Sharia|sharia]]. The state religion is [[Sunni Islam]] and the official language is Malay. Petroleum and natural gas fund a welfare system with free or subsidized housing, healthcare and education. Brunei was a British protectorate from 1888 until it became fully sovereign on January 1, 1984. It is a member of the [[ASEAN]] and the [[United Nations]].

American singer-songwriter and record producer, born Peter Gene Hernandez. Raised in [[Honolulu]], he moved to [[Los Angeles]] in 2003. As a songwriter and co-founder of the production team the Smeezingtons, he became a recording artist. His album *24K Magic* (2016) won the [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]] Award for Album of the Year. His single "Uptown Funk" became Billboard's best-performing song of the 2010s. He has sold more than 150 million records, and [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named him among the 100 most influential people in the world in 2011.

Tool with bristles, wire or other filaments set into a handle or block. Brushes clean, groom [[Hair|hair]], apply [[Cosmetics|makeup]], and serve for [[Painting|painting]] and surface finishing; a household may contain several dozen varieties. Brushmaking dates to ancient Egypt around 3500 BC, when paint brushes were made from split palm leaves and animal hair. The first mass-produced toothbrush appeared in the 1700s. Metal ferrules improved durability, and in 1859 the first brush factory in America was set up in New York. Modern brushes may use [[Nylon|nylon]] or [[Polypropylene|polypropylene]] filaments.

Federal region of central Belgium, including the capital (pop., 2024: 1,255,795). It is the de facto capital of the [[European Union]], hosting its principal institutions, and it is the headquarters of [[NATO]]. Historically Dutch-speaking, it shifted to French from the late 19th century. It has been officially bilingual in French and Dutch since 1989, though French is the majority language and [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]]. Its landmarks include the Grand-Place, the Atomium and Manneken Pis, and some are [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]]. The Brussels Metro is the only [[Rapid transit|rapid transit]] system in Belgium.

Cultivar group of [[Cabbage|cabbage]] (*Brassica oleracea*) grown for its edible buds. The sprouts resemble miniature cabbages and grow in spirals along tall stalks. The vegetable was cultivated near [[Brussels]], Belgium, in the 13th century, and the name derives from there; the first written reference dates to 1587. It reached Britain by the 17th century. Like [[Broccoli]] and [[Kale]], it is cruciferous. An 80 g serving contains more [[Vitamin C|vitamin C]] than an orange.

Canadian singer-songwriter, record producer and photographer. He is estimated to have sold 75 million to more than 100 million records and singles. His 1984 album *Reckless* was the first album by a Canadian to be certified diamond in Canada. His 1991 single "(Everything I Do) I Do It for You" was number one in the United Kingdom for 16 consecutive weeks. He has won Juno Awards and a Grammy Award, and he was nominated for three [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for songwriting for films. He has been inducted into the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

American actor known for both comic and dramatic work on stage and screen. He first gained prominence as Hal in the sitcom *Malcolm in the Middle* (2000–2006). He played Walter White in [[Breaking Bad]] (2008–2013), winning four Primetime Emmy Awards for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series. He won Tony Awards for playing [[Lyndon B. Johnson]] in *All the Way* (2014) and Howard Beale in *Network*. He was nominated for an Academy Award and a British Academy Film Award for his portrayal of Dalton Trumbo in *Trumbo* (2015).

Group of non-[[Vascular tissue|vascular]] land plants comprising [[Liverwort|liverworts]], [[Hornwort|hornworts]] and [[Moss|mosses]]. Bryophytes are small and prefer moist habitats, though some species survive drier conditions. They produce enclosed reproductive structures but no flowers or [[Seed|seeds]]. They reproduce sexually by [[Spore|spores]] and asexually by fragmentation or gemmae. Their life cycles are dominated by the haploid [[Gametophyte|gametophyte]], on which the diploid [[Sporophyte|sporophyte]] remains dependent. Because they do not rely on roots, they can grow where vascular plants cannot. The name comes from Ancient Greek *brúon* ('tree moss, liverwort') and *phutón* ('plant'). Sperm are flagellated and must swim to archegonia, which may be on a different plant.
